top_evidence.document_title: Identifying existing approaches used to evaluate the sustainability of evidence-based interventions in healthcare: an integrative review Check for updates
top_evidence.text: Background: There is limited evidence to evaluate the sustainability of evidence-based interventions (EBIs) for healthcare improvement. Through an integrative review, we aimed to identify approaches to evaluate the sustainability of evidence-based interventions (EBIs) and sustainability outcomes. Methods: Following Whittemore and Knafl's methodological process: (1) problem identification; (2) literature search; (3) data evaluation; (4) data analysis; and (5) presentation, a comprehensive search strategy was applied across five databases. Included studies were not restricted by research design; and had to evaluate the sustainability of an EBI in a healthcare context. We assessed the methodological quality of studies using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Results: Of 18,783 articles retrieved, 64 fit the inclusion criteria. Qualitative designs were most commonly used for evaluation (48%), with individual interviews as the predominant data collection method. Timing of data collection varied widely with post-intervention data collection most frequent (89%). Of the 64 studies, 44% used a framework, 26% used a model, 11% used a tool, 5% used an instrument, and 14% used theory as their primary approach to evaluate sustainability. Most studies (77%) did not measure sustainability outcomes, rather these studies focused on sustainability determinants. Discussion: It is unclear which approach/approaches are most effective for evaluating sustainability and what measures and outcomes are most commonly used. There is a disconnect between evaluating the factors that may shape sustainability and the outcomes approaches employed to measure sustainability. Our review offers methodological recommendations for sustainability evaluation research and highlights the importance in understanding mechanisms of sustainability to advance the field. understand ways to improve the implementation and dissemination of EBIs in healthcare [2]. As IS has matured, researchers have recognized that implementation, which often requires substantial resources, is meaningless without long-term sustainability efforts [3]. We draw upon a comprehensive definition for sustainability by Moore et al. top_evidence.document_title: Identifying existing approaches used to evaluate the sustainability of evidence-based interventions in healthcare: an integrative review Check for updates
top_evidence.text: We conducted a systematic database search using comprehensive strategies, including diverse data sources and methodologies, to advance the understanding of sustainability evaluation as it relates to health EBIs. In December 2018 and July 2020, we searched the following databases: Ovid MEDLINE(R) and Epub Ahead of Print, In-Process and Other Non-Indexed Citations and Daily (1946 to current); OVID Embase (1974 to current); EBSCOhost CINAHL Plus with Full-text (1937 to current); Wiley Cochrane Library (inception to current). A The two reviewers independently extracted the following variables: (1) study design, (2) evaluation type (independent versus composite), (3) sustainability definition and terms used, (4) type and name of theoretical approach, (5) purpose of approach use, (6) data collection Table 1 Inclusion and exclusion criteria a Defined as a process for describing and/or guiding the process of translating research into practice (process models); understanding and/or explaining what influences implementation outcomes (determinant frameworks, classic theories, implementation theories); and evaluating implementation (evaluation frameworks) [14] b Defined as a theoretical approach in implementation science with some predictive capacity (e.g., to what extent … ?) and attempts to provide an enhanced understanding and explanation of certain aspects of implementation [14] c Defined as a theoretical approach in implementation science commonly used to describe and/or guide the specific, step-by-step, process of translating research into practice [14] d Defined as a theoretical approach in implementation science with a descriptive purpose [14]. Points out factors believed or found to influence implementation outcomes but does not specify the mechanisms of change [14] e Facilitates evaluation and usually evolves as an extension of frameworks, or models, or to operationalize theories [14] f Assists individuals on how to retrieve, comprehend, and implement research evidence [14] g Defined as a broad array of services and places where healthcare provision occurs, including acute care hospitals, urgent care centers, rehabilitation centers, nursing homes and other long-term care facilities, specialized outpatient services (e.g., hemodialysis, dentistry, podiatry, chemotherapy, endoscopy, and pain management clinics), and outpatient surgery centers methods, (7) timing of evaluation data collection (e.g., pre-, and/or post-implementation of intervention), (8) reported sustainability measures and, 9. reported sustainability outcomes.

top_evidence.document_title: Identifying existing approaches used to evaluate the sustainability of evidence-based interventions in healthcare: an integrative review Check for updates
top_evidence.text: We conducted an integrative review that followed Whittemore and Knafl's [12] five-stage methodological process: (1) problem identification; (2) literature search; (3) data evaluation; (4) data analysis (data reduction, display, comparison, and conclusions); and (5) presentation. Integrative reviews can include diverse data sources and do not restrict the type of study design. Furthermore, integrative reviews take a more flexible approach to analysis compared to systematic reviews, combining both quantitative and qualitative data if there are similarities [12-14].

top_evidence.document_title: Identifying existing approaches used to evaluate the sustainability of evidence-based interventions in healthcare: an integrative review Check for updates
top_evidence.text: We used Endnote X7 as the management system for this review. After removing duplicates, we conducted a two-stage screening process of the citations retrieved from our database searches. In the first screening stage, one reviewer (RF) independently screened the abstracts and titles of all the citations retrieved from the database searches. A second reviewer (AB) independently screened a randomly selected 10% of all titles and abstracts to verify selection for inclusion or exclusion. In the second stage, two reviewers (RF and AB) independently screened all full-text articles that had passed first-stage screening. We discussed any differences in screening at team meetings and refined our inclusion and exclusion criteria to reflect these discussions.

top_evidence.document_title: Identifying existing approaches used to evaluate the sustainability of evidence-based interventions in healthcare: an integrative review Check for updates
top_evidence.text: We extracted whether an included study evaluated (a) sustainability determinants and (b) sustainability outcomes and how they measured these variables. We defined sustainability determinants as correlates and predictors of sustainability (organizational, contextual, and strategies) and sustainability outcomes as the subsequent impact (healthcare improvement or public health outcomes) of sustained intervention use [5]. To further unpack sustainability outcomes, we extracted and synthesized nine sustainability outcomes across the 64 included studies (Table 3) [6, 15, 16]. Table 2 Categories of theoretical approaches used in implementation science Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) guidelines flow diagram [18]. Our results are presented under five headings according to our research aims. Full citation list for the 64 studies can be found in Additional file 3. Data analysis followed the methodological steps outlined by Whittemore and Knafl [12] which included data reduction, data display, data comparison, and drawing conclusions and verifications. We compared, grouped, and synthesized each study by these variables. Evidence tables were created to summarize and describe the studies included in this review.

elements.quote: Our synthesis indicated that there is a breadth of theoretical approaches and constructs that were considered for the evaluation of the sustainability of EBIs in healthcare that were consistent with other recent synthesis work [6-10]. A recent scoping review and theory analysis [8] found 37 sustainability determinant factors, which grouped into seven themes: (1) characteristics of the innovation / EBP; (2) adopter/user factors influencing sustained use (3) leadership and management influences/factors; (4) inner context (practice setting/organization) factors where EBPs are delivered; (5) inner processes / infrastructure factors that support the EBPs (e.g., processes, methods, systems, structures, or strategies); (6) outer context or broader system factors; and (7) outcomes descriptions without defined factors. These themes are similar to the work of Lennox et al. Most sustainability evaluations included in this study used qualitative research designs (48%), with interviews as the most common data collection method. This finding is consistent with the work of Lennox [6] who reported 59% of their included studies used qualitative methods.
elements.reason: The authors explicitly interpret their results by comparing them to prior syntheses and specific studies (e.g., Lennox et al., a recent scoping review), noting consistency and situating their findings within existing evidence.

elements.quote: Based upon the findings of our review we can offer some key methodological guidance for evaluations of the sustainability of EBIs in healthcare. Firstly, we recommend where feasible to use a combination of approaches for evaluating sustainability of EBIs. A combination of approaches that can evaluate sustainability determinant and outcomes will facilitate our understanding of linkages between determinants and patient or system level outcomes. Secondly, we recommend mixed-methods approach for sustainability evaluation. Mixed methods research designs can provide a better understanding of complex phenomena. Thirdly, we recommend evaluations of sustainability at multiple time points, including pre-intervention in order understand the evolution of sustainability over time.

elements.quote: Additional file 3. Citation list of included studies. A citation list of all included studies ( n = 64). They are listed in alphabetical order, according to the Vancouver referencing style.
elements.reason: The manuscript provides a complete citation list for all included studies (n=64) via Additional file 3.

elements.quote: The research designs and MMAT [18] quality appraisal scores of the included studies are presented in Table 8. The scale ranges from 100 (highest quality) to 0% (lowest quality); however, all included studies ranged from 100 to 40%.
elements.reason: The evidence indicates that some study characteristics (e.g., research design and MMAT quality score) are presented in a table (Table 8), but it does not explicitly show that key characteristics for every included study are presented in a comparison table/figure.
No evidence was retrieved showing that, for an intervention review, intervention details for every study are summarized in an additional table.

elements.quote: The research designs and MMAT [18] quality appraisal scores of the included studies are presented in Table 8.
elements.reason: The evidence indicates that an overall methodological quality score (MMAT) is presented (Table 8), but it does not explicitly report domain-level and overall risk-of-bias judgements for each included study.
No evidence was retrieved showing that justifications for each risk-of-bias judgement are presented for every included study.
No evidence was retrieved that outcome-specific risk-of-bias judgements are displayed alongside study results.
No evidence is provided that, for every outcome and study, appropriate group-level summary statistics for each group are reported.
No evidence is provided that, for every outcome and study, an effect estimate and a measure of precision (e.g., confidence/credible interval) are reported.

elements.quote: Figure 2 depicts the distribution of reported sustainability outcomes. The outcomes reported in each of the 64 included studies can be found in Additional file 4.
elements.reason: A visual result is presented (Figure 2). The manuscript indicates corresponding study-level tabular information exists in Additional file 4, but the retrieved evidence does not show the table itself or confirm it is a tabular presentation of the same results in the sense required for outcomes/effect estimates.
No evidence is provided about reporting the source of study-level data when multiple data sources were used.
No evidence is provided identifying which results were computed/estimated rather than directly reported.

elements.quote: The research designs and MMAT [18] quality appraisal scores of the included studies are presented in Table 8. The scale ranges from 100 (highest quality) to 0% (lowest quality); however, all included studies ranged from 100 to 40%. More than half (59%; n = 38) of included studies received a quality appraisal score of 100%, indicating the included studies are of high methodological quality.
elements.reason: The review reports methodological quality (MMAT scores) for included studies, but it does not explicitly provide risk of bias (nor clearly link the quality/risk information to each specific synthesis).
The retrieved evidence does not identify which specific studies contributed to each synthesis (no synthesis-specific study lists are provided in the evidence supplied).
No evidence is provided that results of any pre-specified or additional statistical syntheses (if conducted) are reported.
The retrieved evidence does not report any meta-analysis summary estimates and their precision.
The retrieved evidence does not report any measures of statistical heterogeneity for meta-analyses.
No evidence is provided for synthesized results and precision (or equivalent information) for other statistical synthesis methods.
No evidence is provided for results from synthesis methods without an effect estimate, including relevant statistics and question-consistent interpretation.
The retrieved evidence does not describe any group comparisons or the direction of effect.
No mean-difference synthesis details (scale units, limits, direction of benefit, or minimally important difference) are reported in the retrieved evidence.
No re-expressed standardized mean difference synthesis details (target instrument information) are reported in the retrieved evidence.
No evidence is provided describing results of investigations of possible causes of heterogeneity among study results (e.g., subgroup/meta-regression/other heterogeneity investigations).
No evidence is provided identifying studies contributing to each subgroup.
No evidence is provided interpreting heterogeneity analyses with attention to observational nature and possible confounding.
No evidence is provided for subgroup analyses reporting interaction-test P values, subgroup estimates, precision, and heterogeneity.
No evidence is provided reporting the difference between subgroup effects and its precision.
No evidence is provided for meta-regression results reporting coefficient P values and precision.
No evidence is provided presenting meta-regression scatterplots.
No evidence is provided describing results of informal heterogeneity investigations.
No results of any sensitivity analyses are reported in the provided evidence.
The provided evidence does not discuss robustness of the main analysis in light of any sensitivity analyses.
No comparison of original and sensitivity-analysis results (including assumptions and contributing studies) in tables is shown in the provided evidence.
The provided evidence includes no forest plots displaying sensitivity-analysis results.
No evidence was retrieved showing that risk of bias due to missing results (arising from reporting biases) was assessed for each synthesis.
No evidence was retrieved indicating that any tool was used for risk-of-bias assessments of missing results, nor any item responses/judgements/supporting information.
No evidence was retrieved of funnel plot use or reporting of funnel plot/estimate/precision/contour milestones.
No evidence was retrieved of a funnel-plot asymmetry test or any reported exact P value/statistics.
No evidence was retrieved of sensitivity analyses examining missing results and comparing with a primary analysis.
No evidence was retrieved of selective non-reporting assessments presented in a study-by-synthesis matrix.
No evidence was retrieved of studies with missing results displayed beneath forest plots or in a table.
No overall certainty/confidence level for each important outcome is reported in the provided results evidence.
No reasons for rating certainty down/up are described in the provided evidence.
The provided evidence does not show certainty communicated alongside results using a section-appropriate format.
No evidence summary tables (e.g., GRADE Summary of Findings) are included in the provided material.

elements.quote: Our synthesis indicated that there is a breadth of theoretical approaches and constructs that were considered for the evaluation of the sustainability of EBIs in healthcare that were consistent with other recent synthesis work [6-10].
elements.reason: In the Discussion, the authors compare their synthesized findings to other recent synthesis work and state that their results were consistent with that external evidence.

elements.quote: We only included published studies in the English language and peer-reviewed primary studies in this review. This review entailed a comprehensive search of published literature and rigorous review methods; however, we recognize that there is the possibility of incomplete retrieval of identified research. For example, all gray literature was excluded.
elements.reason: The manuscript discusses limitations related to the included evidence (language restriction to English, exclusion of gray literature, and potential incomplete retrieval).

elements.quote: This review entailed a comprehensive search of published literature and rigorous review methods; however, we recognize that there is the possibility of incomplete retrieval of identified research. For example, all gray literature was excluded.

elements.quote: This review entailed a comprehensive search of published literature and rigorous review methods; however, we recognize that there is the possibility of incomplete retrieval of identified research. For example, all gray literature was excluded.
elements.reason: The potential limitation(s) are described, but the evidence does not clearly discuss the potential impact of each limitation (e.g., how excluding gray literature or incomplete retrieval might affect findings or conclusions).

elements.quote: Such evidence would also support the sustainability of the EBI in practice [35].
elements.reason: The authors link the need for multiple time points/measurement to sustaining an EBI in practice, but this is limited and does not broadly discuss implications for practice.
No retrieved evidence explicitly discusses implications of the results for policy.

elements.quote: Primary research to compare theoretical approaches used in sustainability evaluation research, to which determinants are most pertinent to sustainability evaluation is non-existent.
elements.reason: This explicitly identifies a need for future research to address a knowledge gap.
